title: Evaluating Attention Through Film
text_snippet: Evaluating Attention Through Film Abstract Being able to evaluate the quality of a subject’s attention is important for students in a contemporary technological society where attention is a highly sought after commodity. I argue that evaluating attention can be particularly effective through engaging with film, especially considering the increasing challenges that undergraduate students face in relation to attention and technology (e.g., pausing the scroll and staying immersed in reading and writing). This pedagogical approach empowers students to be able to philosophically evaluate attention in the context of contemporary technological use by engaging with relevant examples from film.

title: Polycrisis, Happiness and Resilience: Aristotle Indigenized
text_snippet: Polycrisis, Happiness and Resilience: Aristotle Indigenized Abstract The polycrisis demands of educational theory a heightened awareness of ethical and political complexities. We argue that Aristotle’s philosophy enhances this awareness, provided we move beyond standard readings that focus on virtue ethics in idealized conditions of normality. Specifically, we show that the Aristotelian distinction between eudaimonia and makariotes clarifies ethico-political stakes across a wide spectrum of existential conditions, extending all the way to kakodaimonia and catastrophe. For Aristotle, makariotes is the ultimate regulative ideal of education, while eudaimonia remains the more feasible aim in conditions of adversity. By historicizing Aristotle’s terms within their original Greek context, we contest the modern, domesticating filters that flatten the makariotes-eudaimonia distinction. We conclude by leveraging this distinction to conceptualize resilience as survivance beyond current emphases on adaptability.

title: ‘Seeing Like a Movie’: Cultivating the Poetic Gaze with Thomas Aquinas and the Artform of the Moving Image
text_snippet: ‘Seeing Like a Movie’: Cultivating the Poetic Gaze with Thomas Aquinas and the Artform of the Moving Image Abstract Why does Aquinas go to the movies and what does all of this have to do with education? In order to shed light on this productive confusion, I shall explore Thomas Aquinas’ medieval notion of divine poiesis not merely as a theological or metaphysical intrusion of the pedagogical field, but as a model and metaphor that philosophises on the nature, purpose and practice of human self-formation. In the first part, I draw on John Milbank and Catherine Pickstock’s Truth in Aquinas and Jacques Maritain’s work on the virtue of art. For St Thomas, human beings do not only participate in the act of divine creativity by the fact of their created-ness. By imitation of God’s free, self-forgetting aesthetic movement from idea to form (modelled in the creation, the incarnation), humans—with the artist as the key example—are to cultivate their mimetic capacity for a ‘simple’ aesthetic seeing-as-making. Having laid out Aquinas’ philosophy of human formation, I will then, in the second part, enlist the help of film phenomenologist Vivian Sobchack. title: Alternative Conceptions of Interdisciplinarity in Educational Research: A Philosophical Analysis
text_snippet: Alternative Conceptions of Interdisciplinarity in Educational Research: A Philosophical Analysis Abstract Interdisciplinarity in school settings is frequently described in educational literature as aconcept with multiple or competing meanings, yet these claims have rarely beenexamined through systematic analysis of research discourse itself. This paperinvestigates how interdisciplinarity is understood through its use within a corpus ofeducational research. Drawing on contextualized conceptual analysis informed byordinary language philosophy, the study analyses all occurrences of the term in theselected studies rather than focusing only on explicit definitions. The analysis identifiesthree recurring dimensions structuring its use: teleological (educational aims),procedural (forms of disciplinary connection), and material (school disciplines). Withinthe teleological and procedural dimensions, distinct orientations emerge, reflectingdifferent understandings of the purposes and scope of interdisciplinarity. Theircombinations yield six recurring configurations of use, which serve as a heuristic mapof the concept’s logic of use rather than as fixed categories or a new stipulativedefinition. title: When Experience Miseducates: Dewey, Gadamer and the Problem of Openness
text_snippet: When Experience Miseducates: Dewey, Gadamer and the Problem of Openness Abstract Experience is often treated as a pedagogical good, associated with activity, authenticity, participation, learning and growth. Yet experience can also miseducate by narrowing horizons, reinforcing unreflective habits and restricting future possibilities for understanding and judgment. Dewey foregrounds the normative distinction between educative and miseducative experience by linking educational value to the consequences of experience for further growth, while Gadamer clarifies how experience transforms the subject by unsettling prior understanding and opening a changed relation to subject matter, self and the world. The article uses this dialogue to understand miseducation in terms of restricted openness : a form of pedagogical harm in which experience narrows students’ future capacity to understand, judge and respond. The concept of restricted openness specifies a form of miseducation that may remain invisible when educational value is assessed primarily through activity, engagement or intended learning outcomes. title: Educating for Intellectual Character and the AI Revolution in Education
text_snippet: Educating for Intellectual Character and the AI Revolution in Education Abstract While there is widespread agreement that the new AI technology will revolutionize education, the exact nature of why it will have such a dramatic effect is often left unclarified. It is argued that understanding the nature of the AI educational challenge requires us to recognize that the overarching epistemic goal of education is to cultivate intellectual character. This enables us to appreciate how AI poses a very different challenge to education than traditional forms of technology. While one can normally effectively adapt educational practices to new technology, this is not possible in the case of AI due to how it has the potential to deprive students of the cognitive activities that educators use to cultivate intellectual character. With the AI educational challenge so understood, two interconnected strategies of response are proposed: introducing ‘cloistered’ periods of instruction where students are insulated from AI-based technologies, and explicitly teaching students the theory behind educating for intellectual character. title: The Case Against Liberal Global Citizenship Education
text_snippet: The Case Against Liberal Global Citizenship Education Abstract Liberal global citizenship education (GCE) has emerged as a prominent conception of global education, aiming to cultivate universal liberal values in students worldwide. There are two versions: comprehensive GCE, which aims for liberal values in students’ private lives, and political GCE, which restricts education to students’ public lives as citizens. Generally, existing critiques take issue with the theory of liberalism. In this paper, I instead offer an internal objection which holds that liberalism itself does not support liberal GCE. I proceed by objecting to comprehensive and political GCE on the grounds of liberal toleration. I argue that comprehensive GCE is not legitimate, as its parochial values are intolerant of nonliberal comprehensive doctrines. Educating for comprehensive liberal values oversteps legitimate educational justifications. Political GCE, I argue, is intolerant when extended internationally to nonliberal societies. Liberalism must remain tolerant of nonliberal societies and political doctrines out of respect for reasonable alternative values. title: Beyond the Educational Enclosure: Commoning and/or Opening
text_snippet: Beyond the Educational Enclosure: Commoning and/or Opening Abstract This paper begins by introducing the concept of the pedagogy of the common world, situating Morten Korsgaard’s specific interpretation of this pedagogy within contemporary debates that critically examine the notions of progress and enclosure. Against this backdrop, it addresses the question of “commoning” by comparing the perspectives of Arendt and Dewey. It argues, first, that their approaches offer two distinct tonalities in balancing renewal with conservation and continuity in education. Second, despite their significant differences, their conceptual frameworks may share a common root. This shared foundation is explored by drawing on the work of twentieth-century Italian educationalist Aldo Capitini, whose idea of “prophetic education” provides a lens to examine both the differences and the similarities between Deweyan and Arendtian approaches. Capitini’s perspective also suggests the possibility of a form of beginning and commoning that aligns with a sense of progressivity and dynamic growth. title: Socratic or Sophistic AI? A Badiouian Ontological Critique of the Logic of AI-Based Personalized Learning
text_snippet: Socratic or Sophistic AI? A Badiouian Ontological Critique of the Logic of AI-Based Personalized Learning Abstract First, this article aims to contribute to the existing and growing body of literature on Badiou’s philosophy and its relevance for educational philosophy and theory. What is distinctive about a ‘Badiouian’ philosophy of education is his insistence that any education worthy of its name is necessarily ‘an education by truths’ and that there needs to be a clear distinction between the (non-)education of the ‘sophists’ and the education for and by truths of Socrates. The second ambition of this article is to introduce Badiou’s philosophy and a Badiouian philosophy of education into the discussions and debates around the rise of the AI-based personalization of learning. What Badiou’s philosophy could contribute to this body of work is a firmly ontological – as opposed to an epistemological and/or axiological – critique of personalized learning empowered by AI. This article is divided into four parts. First, we provide a concise account of Alain Badiou’s philosophy. We then proceed to identify some features of a ‘Badiouian’ education. title: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Formative Epistemic Injustice, and Educators’ Solutions
text_snippet: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Formative Epistemic Injustice, and Educators’ Solutions Abstract The advent of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has forced educators to contend with its presence in schools, classrooms, and student work. In this paper, I investigate the epistemic consequences of using GenAI in literacy learning. Using the concept of formative epistemic injustice, I argue a wrong is done to students when instructors encourage students to farm out learning tasks to GenAI; specifically, formative epistemic injustice is done to students when they are told to use GenAI. Using the example of writing studies, I show how many of the tasks students and educators are most likely to assign to GenAI when writing are some of the most educative, resulting in formative epistemic injustice when GenAI is used. Recognizing the staying power of GenAI in education and schooling, I sketch out ways to mitigate the mal-formative effects of the use of GenAI in writing classrooms.

title: Human–Nature Relationship in Gramsci: Contributions to Critical Pedagogy and Ecopedagogy
text_snippet: Human–Nature Relationship in Gramsci: Contributions to Critical Pedagogy and Ecopedagogy Abstract This article offers a contemporary reassessment of Antonio Gramsci’s pedagogical perspective on the relationship between human beings and nature, based on selected notes from the Prison Notebooks . The central argument is that such a relationship should not be understood as external or unidirectional, but as a historically mediated dimension constitutive of subjectivity and social life. In this sense, the analysis situates Gramsci’s philosophy of praxis in dialogue with current debates in critical pedagogy and ecopedagogy, showing how his thought contributes to rethinking the socio-environmental question from an educational standpoint. Additionally, the study underscores the relevance of these reflections in contemporary global contexts marked by ecological crisis and political struggles for socio-environmental justice, where educational institutions face demands to develop transformative pedagogical approaches. title: From Thoughtfulness to Resonance? Recasting Pedagogical Tact as Ecological Attunement
text_snippet: From Thoughtfulness to Resonance? Recasting Pedagogical Tact as Ecological Attunement Abstract Abstract This article argues that Hartmut Rosa’s concept of resonance offers a more productive way of rethinking pedagogical tact than Max van Manen’s notion of thoughtfulness. While van Manen’s phenomenology of practice insightfully presents tact as embodied, situational, and ethically responsive, its reliance on thoughtfulness leaves unsolved questions concerning subjectivity, methodological opacity, and the theoretical status of the pedagogical relation. The article first reconstructs the conceptual development of pedagogical tact from Herbart to van Manen, showing how thoughtfulness tends to privilege the educator’s reflective interiority. An argumentative test supports this proposal: the rereading of a scene from Être et avoir , which exposes the limits of a teacher-centred interpretation of tact. title: AI Personalized Learning and the Risk of Epistemic Consolidation
text_snippet: AI Personalized Learning and the Risk of Epistemic Consolidation Abstract Many researchers and industry leaders hold that AI personalized learning systems are about to unleash a better, more flexible, and richly diverse form of instructional support than was experienced by any previous generation of learners. In this essay I grant that AI personalized learning systems may diversify curriculum, instruction, and assessment experiences in a typical classroom. Nevertheless, I argue that efforts to personalize learning by shifting diverse human teachers' work into a smaller number of scalable AI instructional systems can result in a transfer and concentration of human teachers’ previously diffuse and limited pedagogical power over a population’s instructional experiences. I call this process of concentrating power over a population’s instructional experiences the epistemic consolidation of teaching. Highly scalable epistemically consolidated AI teaching systems—capable of shaping (or mishaping) what the public thinks, does, and feels in highly personalized ways—raise new and unique social, political, and epistemic risks. title: Paradise Lost: Significant Otherness in Pedagogical Practice—A Tentacular Exploration
text_snippet: Paradise Lost: Significant Otherness in Pedagogical Practice—A Tentacular Exploration Abstract This paper explores how pedagogical beliefs are challenged in everyday encounters, particularly when someone in an educational relationship acts unexpectedly. Following Donna Haraway’s notion of tentacular thinking (2016), I examine my relationship with Lyra, a reactive dog, as a site where prior experiences, emotions, and social expectations intertwine. The analysis sits at the intersection of social interactionism, posthumanist theory, and post-critical educational research, and incorporates Johan Asplund’s (1987a, b) idea of social responsivity as an elementary form of social life, Haraway’s (2003, 2008) concept of otherness-in-connection, and B. F. Skinner’s (1953) account of operant conditioning. These perspectives provide a lens for understanding how convictions are tested in emotionally charged encounters, and how traditional logics of discipline may resurface, unsettling relational ethics that aim to supplant them. The paper offers insights relevant for teaching, parenting, and multispecies companionships. title: Community and Purpose in the Academy
text_snippet: Community and Purpose in the Academy Abstract References to “the academic community” abound in higher-education discourse, yet the concept itself is rarely examined. This paper argues that academic community is not only an empirical phenomenon but a normative ideal essential to the moral, intellectual, and institutional purposes of higher education. Contemporary universities, however, increasingly undermine the conditions for such community through organizational professionalism, individualism, managerialism, retreat from academic citizenship, and troubled collegiality. Drawing on sociological and normative theories of community, the paper distinguishes between descriptive accounts of academic networks and a richer, value-laden conception grounded in shared purposes, intellectual virtues, and relational practices. A value-theoretical analysis shows that academic community is instrumentally, constitutively, and intrinsically connected to core academic values such as knowledge, understanding, learning, and justice, and that it contributes to human flourishing. title: Time, Signs and Symbols: Toward a Schutzian Phenomenology of Education
text_snippet: Time, Signs and Symbols: Toward a Schutzian Phenomenology of Education Abstract This paper develops a phenomenological framework for exploring how time is experienced in classroom interaction, drawing on Alfred Schutz’s theory of signs, symbols, and multiple realities. While critical studies have shown how clock time shapes schooling through efficiency, standardization, and acceleration, less attention has been given to how educational time is lived as meaningful, shared, or alienating in everyday practice. Responding to calls by scholars such as Barbara Adam for time studies rooted in Schutz, this paper clarifies and operationalizes his concepts of time, symbols, and multiple realities for empirical investigation in educational settings. title: For an Educational Engagement with Crisis
text_snippet: For an Educational Engagement with Crisis Abstract Crisis is an all-embracing phenomenon. Once erupting, it is experienced on many levels and is often felt like no part of life is kept safe from it. When an individual, a group or society as a whole undergo a crisis, not only do they face hardships and threats to their very survival, stability and well-being but they also operate in unique epistemological conditions. While education in times of crisis is often tasked with recruiting students in the efforts to overcome it and with providing them emotional support, I argue that there is another important task that education is uniquely qualified for—operating from within the conditions of crisis and engaging with its epistemological difficulties to achieve better understanding. title: Generative AI and the Irreducible Role of Teachers as Callers into Subjectness: A Placebo–Nocebo–Treatment Framework
text_snippet: Generative AI and the Irreducible Role of Teachers as Callers into Subjectness: A Placebo–Nocebo–Treatment Framework Abstract The current discourse on Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education largely overlooks its potential disruption to what educational philosopher Gert Biesta identifies as one of the irreducible purposes of education. title: Confucian Self-Cultivation and the Ethics of Learning with Large Language Models
text_snippet: Confucian Self-Cultivation and the Ethics of Learning with Large Language Models Abstract The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT has transformed contemporary teaching and learning, raising pressing questions about the moral, relational, and epistemic dimensions of education. This paper examines these challenges through the lens of Confucian ethics, focusing on the moral ideal of self-cultivation and the relational virtues of ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), cheng (sincerity), zhong (loyalty), and shu (empathy). It argues that prevailing Western approaches to AI ethics—grounded in procedural, utilitarian, or rights-based reasoning—tend to overlook the formative and relational nature of moral education. Drawing on classical Confucian texts and contemporary debates on AI in education, the paper proposes a framework for engaging LLMs in ways that nurture moral reflection, communal responsibility, and human–machine harmony. Rather than viewing AI as a threat to authenticity or agency, a Confucian perspective reorients technological use towards the cultivation of moral character and the pursuit of shared human flourishing.

title: Anticipatory Dignity and Digital Meritocracy: Philosophical Reflections on the Algorithmic Transformation of South Korea’s Education System
text_snippet: Anticipatory Dignity and Digital Meritocracy: Philosophical Reflections on the Algorithmic Transformation of South Korea’s Education System Abstract This study introduces “anticipatory dignity” as a fundamental extension of human dignity discourse to address temporal challenges posed by algorithmic prediction in educational settings. Building on Kantian ethics, Feinberg’s “right to an open future”, and Raz’s conception of meaningful autonomy, anticipatory dignity designates the right to maintain cognitive openness against premature algorithmic classification that forecloses developmental possibilities before conscious choice can intervene. This philosophical innovation addresses a critical gap in educational philosophy: existing frameworks lack adequate conceptual resources to protect human agency from predictive systems that transform educational development from open-ended self-discovery into continuous optimization. Analysis of South Korea’s AI Digital Textbook initiative illustrates how machine learning institutionalizes epistemic foreclosure despite promises of objectivity. The research proposes institutional mechanisms including Student Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments and prediction ceilings limiting algorithmic forecasts to developmentally appropriate timeframes. title: The Ethics and Politics of New Brutalism in Education: Infrastructures, Affects, and Insurgent Possibilities
text_snippet: The Ethics and Politics of New Brutalism in Education: Infrastructures, Affects, and Insurgent Possibilities Abstract This paper explores the emergence of new brutalism in education as a political, infrastructural, and affective formation that normalizes hardness and domination. Drawing on Achille Mbembe’s (2024) notion of political brutalism and Michael Truscello's (2020) theorization of infrastructural brutalism, the paper examines how contemporary regimes of governance reconfigure education through violence—epistemic, material, and affective. Two examples—Trump 2.0’s renewed assault on higher education in the United States and Taliban 2.0’s repression of women’s and girls’ education in Afghanistan—illustrate how brutalism functions globally as a mode of affective and ideological control. The analysis advances a vision of anti-brutalist insurgency : an ethical and pedagogical orientation that transforms exposure into solidarity through micro-practices of care, repair, and endurance. The paper concludes by reflecting on what it means to educate ethically in brutal times, nurturing care without denying hardness and reimagining education as a site of collective repair.

title: Teaching Beyond Normalisation: Rethinking Standards-Based Reforms Through Canguilhem
text_snippet: Teaching Beyond Normalisation: Rethinking Standards-Based Reforms Through Canguilhem Abstract Standards-based reforms (SBRs), such as the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (APST), have reshaped teachers’ work and redefined what counts as professional judgement and pedagogic practice. In this paper, we reflect on the logic of remedyism embedded in SBR policies such as the APST, through the theoretical lens of the French philosopher Georges Canguilhem. While such policies are widely understood to normalise teachers’ work in a Foucauldian sense, we argue, following Canguilhem, that it is equally important to foreground pedagogic normativity —that is, the capacity of schools and teachers to create context-specific pedagogic practices and possibilities, within complex social realities, through the creation of their own norms , often in the silence of policy technologies. This conception does not endorse normalisation; rather, it resists the technical and performative deployment of teaching standards in policy enactment, which tends to homogenise, universalise, and standardise pedagogy. title: Advancing Justice in Society: Reframing the Role of Education Through Systems and Complexity Theories
text_snippet: Advancing Justice in Society: Reframing the Role of Education Through Systems and Complexity Theories Abstract Key words: Educational justice, Complexity theory, Non ideal theory, Luhmann, Sen, Education. The aim of this article is to offer a new perspective on the form that distributive justice must take in order to effectively guide education toward creating a more just society. Drawing on systems theory and the study of complex adaptive systems, the article challenges the conventional view that distributive justice in education should be based on fixed and universal ideals. Instead, it proposes a more flexible and context-sensitive understanding of justice that responds to the complex nature of real-world settings. Engaging with Niklas Luhmann’s systems theory and Michael Walzer’s account of pluralism, the article suggests that different principles of justice may be appropriate for various educational contexts or institutional arrangements. It also addresses the philosophical implications of viewing continuous change as a central feature of education, arguing that the pursuit of justice in education should be seen as an ongoing and adaptive process rather than a fixed goal. title: Conceptual Criticism about Philosophical Education
text_snippet: Conceptual Criticism about Philosophical Education Abstract In the face of contentious histories of philosophy, philosophical didactics can shed light on philosophical education in critical and innovative ways. Two case studies will be used to examine and question the relationship between philosophy and its history: Rorty’s Dewey and Cavell’s Emerson. By analyzing them as philosophical figures of thought and distinguishing between hostile and critical philosophical ways of reading, on the one hand, and conservative and innovative philosophical ways of reading, on the other, it is possible to elucidate approaches that are capable of eliciting a particular kind of conceptual critique about philosophical education, which can be called “philosophical sincerity.”

title: Relational (Re)Organization: A Case for a Relational Reading of Relational Pedagogy
text_snippet: Relational (Re)Organization: A Case for a Relational Reading of Relational Pedagogy Abstract Consider Bailey STEM Magnet Middle School in Nashville, TN – a school (re)designed a decade ago to attend to the quality of relation and interaction between and among teachers and students and cultivate the capacity for response-ability: the situated ability to respond rather than react to challenges as opportunities for growth. Bailey was not “turned around” to use the language of educational efficiency and accountability. Rather, it was altered at its core by replacing an organization set up hierarchically and designed to “produce results” (e.g., higher test scores) with a structure designed to enable relationality and response-ability. What follows is a theory-generating, practice-based, and empirically-grounded representation of Bailey’s relationally-focused organizational transformation, arguing that relational pedagogy is not only interpersonal but also structural and institutional. We begin with a brief history of Relational Pedagogy. title: Critical Pedagogy Between Modern Commitments and Poststructuralist Challenges in Contemporary Education
text_snippet: Critical Pedagogy Between Modern Commitments and Poststructuralist Challenges in Contemporary Education Abstract This paper examines the evolving relationship between modernity, poststructuralism, and critical pedagogy through the lens of Henry Giroux's educational thought. The central aim is to reassess the epistemological foundations of critical pedagogy in the face of contemporary challenges such as cultural fragmentation, rising authoritarianism, and the erosion of democratic public institutions. Rejecting simplistic binaries between modernity and 'postmodernism', the article argues that Giroux's work articulates a form of pedagogy that is deeply rooted in the critical legacy of philosophical modernity while being responsive to the insights and critiques of poststructuralist thought. The first section reconstructs the modernist foundations of Giroux's pedagogy, shaped by Enlightenment ideals of critique, agency, and rationality, as well as by the Frankfurt School’s commitment to emancipation. The second section investigates how Giroux's later work engages with the challenges posed by poststructuralist theory.
